title: Teacher Workflow No. 07
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), November 2, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel argues that the first five minutes of class are the only time all week when every student is awake and looking at you, yet most teachers spend them on logistics. His workflow turns material teachers already have, namely last week’s exit ticket patterns, the week’s topics, one real headline and older retrieval questions, into three options per class meeting: a misconception rerun, a headline hook and a retrieval pull. The post supplies the exact chat prompt for generating the options, then a verification stage in which the teacher checks only the chosen openers against the source data. A short prompt formats the picks into a one-page card with a fallback for each day, and a Friday tally of what landed feeds into the next week’s input. The total is about twenty Sunday minutes, with an eight-minute minimal version for one class.
points: Exit tickets, a pasted headline and older retrieval questions give the AI real classroom evidence, and the tool is never allowed to invent the headline or facts.
Three opener types (misconception rerun, headline hook, retrieval pull) are each tied to a specific check the teacher performs before using them.

Verification is the stopping point for trust: confirm the rerun targets the actual wrong idea, cut any number or name not in the pasted paragraph, and answer the retrieval question cold to be sure it is not a lookup.
The Friday tally of landed, flat, or ran long feeds the next Sunday’s prompt, so the tool drafts from a term of evidence by week twelve.
quotes: Those are the only minutes all week when every student is awake and looking at you. You spend them on logistics.
The material for a real opener is already on your desk. Last week’s exit tickets told you exactly where the room got lost, and the news did something in your field this week.
copy the headline, the first paragraph, and the URL. The tool never gets to invent one.
The misconception rerun: read it against the pattern it says it targets. The tool likes the neighboring idea, the one that’s easier to write.
Any number, name, or cause that isn’t in the paragraph gets cut, however good it sounds.
If the answer is sitting in the notes a student would have open on the desk, it’s a lookup, and a lookup teaches nothing. Rewrite it so the answer has to come out of a head.
By week twelve the tool is drafting from a term of evidence about what wakes your room up.
Do it tonight, and Monday starts with the room arguing about the exact thing they got wrong on Thursday, before you’ve said a word about chapter ten.
